# 1 · What this course is {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The organising question

> ### When can a number about the past be used to make a claim about the future?

::: {.step}
Every method in the eleven sessions that follow is an answer to some version of that question —
and every one of them comes with conditions.
:::

::: {.tight}
- Twelve sessions, each **90 minutes of teaching + 90 minutes of group work**
- Every method **derived before it is used**
- Everything runs **on your machine**, with open tools
- No API key, no subscription, no internet needed during a practice
:::

## What makes this course unusual

::: {.step}
You are expected to work with a **language model** throughout. It is a required tool, not a
tolerated one.
:::

::: {.warn}
And the standing rule: **every deliverable must document at least one instance where you identified
an LLM output as wrong, unverifiable, or misleading** — and explain how you established that.
:::

::: {.check}
You are never penalised for using the model. You are penalised for using it **uncritically**.
:::

## Why that rule is the point

::: {.step}
Language models made information abundant. They did not make abundant the ability to **ask the
right question** or to **recognise a wrong answer**. Both are functions of expertise.
:::

::: {.muted}
A concrete case, from Session 05. Ask a model to select variables and it will run a lasso and hand
you a list. The list looks authoritative. Only if you know the lasso is unstable under correlated
predictors will you ask the follow-up that matters — *"how often is each of these selected across
bootstrap replicates?"* — and turn a misleading answer into a useful one.
:::

::: {.warn}
The model will not volunteer that question. **You have to know enough to ask.**
:::

# 2 · The twelve sessions {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The arc

| | Session | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **02** | Exploratory data analysis, and the first model | What does the data look like? |
| **03** | Regression: adequacy, validity, robustness | Can the model be trusted? |
| **04** | Logistic regression | The outcome is a category. Now what? |
| **05** | Ridge, lasso, elastic net | Which few indicators carry the signal? |
| **06** | Regression: advanced considerations | Does it hold across countries and years? |

::: {.muted}
**Midterm after Session 06** — on paper, closed book.
:::

## The arc, continued

| | Session | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **07** | Principal component and factor analyses | How many things are being measured? |
| **08** | KNN and the bias–variance trade-off | Flexible, or just unstable? |
| **09** | Structural equation modelling | Can you measure the unobservable? |
| **10** | Causal inference I — matching | Did the policy do anything? |
| **11** | Causal inference II — difference-in-differences | What would have happened otherwise? |
| **12** | Final group presentations | Can you make someone act on this? |

::: {.check}
Sessions 2–6 build the model and test it. Sessions 7–9 find structure nobody labelled. Sessions
10–11 confront the question the first nine cannot answer: whether anything **caused** anything.
:::

## How a session works

| Phase | | What |
|---|---|---|
| **Before** | ~60–90 min | Read the paper. Load its data. Attempt the self-check |
| **First half** | 90 min | Lecture: the method, derived and then run in Python |
| **Second half** | 90 min | Your group applies it to **your own project** |
| **Last 20 min** | | Two-minute reports — presenter drawn **at random** |

::: {.warn}
The presenter is drawn when your group is called. All three of you must understand the analysis,
the number, and what would undermine it.
:::

# 3 · How you are judged {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The four evaluations

| Component | Weight | Form |
|---|---|---|
| **Participation** | **10%** | individual, continuous |
| **Midterm exam** | **30%** | individual, on paper — pen and calculator only |
| **Team work** | **20%** | groups of three, Session 12 |
| **Final exam** | **40%** | **individual** research paper (25) + individual oral, 15 min (15) |

::: {.check}
Two are individual and carry **70%**. The group cannot carry you, and you cannot carry the group.
:::

## Participation — 10%

::: {.step}
Attendance is assumed, so participation cannot mean turning up. It means **contributing to the
room**: a question that changed how another group saw their result, a connection between two
angles, a correction that landed.
:::

::: {.check}
Graded against an **absolute, published bar** — never against each other. Every one of you can earn
full marks.
:::

::: {.warn}
Failing to deliver the two-minute report when drawn is the clearest participation failure there is.
:::

## Midterm — 30%

::: {.tight}
- **On paper. Pen, and a simple four-function calculator**
- No computer, no phone, no internet, no notes
- Two hours, covering **Sessions 1–6**
- Working is marked: a correct answer with no derivation earns part marks
:::

::: {.warn}
**No machine, and no assistant.** Every other assessment assumes a model beside you, because that
is how the work is now done. This one deliberately does not.
:::

::: {.check}
It is the only instrument that isolates what **you** can derive unaided — which is the thing that
lets you tell when the assistant is wrong, for the rest of your career.
:::

## Team work — 20%

| | |
|---|---|
| Model governance file | 7 |
| Reproducible analysis | 7 |
| Revised Session 1 memo + change log | 3 |
| Presentation and defence | 3 |

::: {.step}
Eleven weeks with a **real client**: a student in the SDAfrique programme who identified the problem
and will use what you produce. She is your client, **not your co-author**.
:::

::: {.muted}
An individual multiplier from confidential peer ratings, gated on the git history, applies to this
20% **only** — never to the midterm, never to the final.
:::

::: {.muted}
Default ×1.00. A mark is reduced only when two independent records agree.
:::

## Final exam — 40%

::: {.tight}
- **Research paper**, written **alone** — **25**
- **Individual oral**, 15 minutes, no documents — **15**
:::

::: {.step}
The paper is a methods paper written for a real reader: an SDAfrique student in Benin who works in
R, on a modest machine, with limited bandwidth, on a problem she chose herself.
:::

::: {.warn}
A paper is written slowly, with help, over weeks. **Fifteen minutes without documents** establishes
what you can reconstruct and defend in real time — which is what a referee or an employer actually
tests.
:::

# 4 · Working with a language model {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The rule, as a publisher states it

::: {.step}
This course applies the standard **Elsevier** and **Emerald** apply to submitted work.
:::

::: {.tight}
- AI may be used to **improve readability and language** — not to produce findings
- **Authors are fully responsible** for the content, including anything the tool produced
- Use must be **disclosed** — what tool, for what, where
- AI **cannot be an author**. Authorship implies responsibility a tool cannot hold
:::

::: {.warn}
It is a **research assistant**, not a co-author. It does not do the job; it helps you do the job.
:::

## What that means in practice

::: {.check}
**Ask it to argue against you.** Its most useful output is an objection you had not considered.
:::

::: {.tight}
- Verify every factual claim — especially library APIs, statistical results and citations
- It will state plausible falsehoods with complete confidence
- **Record what you checked**, and how
:::

::: {.muted}
Every deliverable carries an LLM statement: what you used, for what, and the one output you caught
being wrong.
:::

## Ethics and integrity

::: {.step}
HEC Montréal's *Règlement sur les fraudes et plagiat* applies in full. Two clarifications specific
to this course:
:::

::: {.tight}
- **Model use is permitted and expected**, subject to the documentation rule. Presenting model
  output as your own reasoning, without that verification, is **misrepresentation**
- **Code from any source may be used with attribution.** Copy a Stack Overflow answer, cite it in a
  comment. Unattributed borrowing is plagiarism; attributed borrowing is normal practice
:::

::: {.warn}
All data in this course are public. Respect each licence, record provenance, and check before
redistributing anything.
:::

# 5 · What I expect {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four expectations

::: {.tight}
1. **Arrive prepared.** The paper read, the data loaded, the self-check attempted
2. **Say the units.** A coefficient without units is not a finding
3. **State what your result does not license.** Every deliverable in this course asks for it
4. **Push your own commits.** Everyone in the group, every session. The log is the record
:::

::: {.check}
And one more, which is the hardest: **a well-argued refusal earns full marks.** "This cannot be
claimed, and here is what would be needed" is the answer I am looking for.
:::

## What loses marks, everywhere

::: {.tight}
- A number reported without its uncertainty
- An association described in causal language
- A model chosen because it gave the answer you wanted
- An LLM output used without a verification you can point to
- A result that does not reproduce from a clean clone
:::

::: {.warn}
A result that does not reproduce is not a result. That is not pedantry — it is the standard every
serious journal now applies.
:::
